title: the birth of the cousins
hook: the younger widow turns pale, the elder sends her maid in her place, and three very different brothers are born

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth of the cousins began: Ambika shut her eyes, and Dhritarashtra was born blind — a widow too frightened to look. What did you look at straight on? Day seven hundred twenty-three.

Same palace, same sage, a different widow. Satyavati sends Vyasa to the younger princess, Ambalika. When she sees him, the blood leaves her face, and she goes pale. She doesn't shut her eyes, as her sister did. Her fear shows on her face instead. Three women, three answers to the same frightening guest, and the Kuru house is about to get its three brothers: the blind one, the pale one, and one nobody planned for at all.
screen: `A DIFFERENT WIDOW.` → `SHE GOES PALE.` → `ONE NOBODY PLANNED FOR.`

segments.voice: Vyasa tells his mother: because she turned pale, the son will be pale, and that will be his name. Pandu, the pale one. He will be a mighty prince, Vyasa says, and his own sons will be great. So now there are two heirs, one blind and one pale. And Satyavati, still not at peace, asks Vyasa for one more son from the elder widow. But Ambika can't face him again. She remembers his face and his smell, and she does something no one expected: she dresses her maid in her own ornaments, and sends her in her place. The maid isn't afraid. She rises when he enters, greets him with respect, and serves him. And Vyasa is pleased with her. He tells her: you are no longer a servant. And your son will be virtuous and wise. He then tells his mother everything: how the princess deceived him, and how the maid honored him. Then he goes back to the forest. That son is Vidura. The text later explains that he is the god of dharma himself, born as a man because of a sage's curse; that's a story for another day. So here they are, the three brothers. One can't see. One is pale. And the one born of a woman who simply showed respect, the son of a servant, will grow up to be the palace's voice of wisdom, and, because of his mother's place, the one who can never be king. This is the generation before the cousins. Their sons are the ones who will meet on the field.
screen: `PANDU, THE PALE ONE.` · `A MAID IN THE PRINCESS'S JEWELS.` · `SHE GREETS HIM WITH RESPECT.` · `VIDURA, THE WISE ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. The maid met a strange, rough figure and answered him with respect, and it changed her life. Bring to mind someone who makes you uncomfortable: the way they look, or talk, or carry themselves. No need to like them. Just hold them in mind, and try greeting them inwardly, as the maid did: you're welcome here. Notice what tightens, and what eases. Breathe in on their face. Breathe out on the greeting. The bell holds the time.
Pandu, the pale one, born because his mother's face went white with fear, now one of three brothers: the blind, the pale, and the wise.
Your line: she simply showed him respect. Today, greet one person you'd rather avoid as if they were welcome. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 723 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BIRTH OF THE COUSINS.`

howItsDone: Vidura's counsel to the king, the Vidura Niti in the Udyoga Parva, is read by some Hindus as a short guide to wise and honest living.

pairs: the maid's son, the wise one
turned pale at the sight of Vyasa

myth: Ambika went to Vyasa a second time
she sent her maid, dressed in her own ornaments.
Vyasa was angry with the maid
he was pleased, freed her from service, and blessed her son.
and the text says her son would be wise and virtuous.

fork.setup: you're Ambika. Satyavati asks you to receive the frightening sage again. what do you do?
options: go again, eyes open this time.
send your maid, in your own jewels.
fork.reveal: she sends her maid, who greets Vyasa with respect, and Vidura is born.

original.note: Sanskrit Pandu: the pale one, the name Vyasa gives Ambalika's son because she turned pale.

trapdoor: what you thought: three princes born in a palace.
what it means: three sons shaped by fear, by pallor, and by a servant's respect.
what a scholar hears: the text later says Vidura is dharma itself, born as a man under a sage's curse.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Ambalika and the birth of Pandu; the maid sent by Ambika and the birth of Vidura)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Vidura as Dharma, cursed by the sage Animandavya)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Ambalika's pallor and Vyasa naming the son Pandu for it; Ambika's substitution of her maid adorned in her ornaments; the maid's respectful welcome; Vyasa freeing her from servitude and praising the coming son; Vyasa telling Satyavati of the deception.
Vyasa's blessing on the son is softened to 'virtuous and wise'; Ganguli's wording is stronger and was not used under the no-superlatives rule.
Vidura as an incarnation of Dharma under Animandavya's curse is only mentioned, not told.
The maid is described as a Sudra woman in the text; the script says 'servant' and 'mother's place'. A Keeper may wish to address caste more directly or not at all.
howItsDone names the Vidura Niti; confirm placement in the Udyoga Parva and phrasing.

Editor pass: hook no longer says Ambalika was told about her sister or that all three choices happened in one night (neither is in the text); 'Ambika agrees' cut, since in Ganguli she does not consent to a second meeting.
